blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nurse Williams, we had, I think, yesterday finished looking at the observation chart that you had completed and which began at 02.45. Just staying with some of the records that you made, please, I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to put up tile 37 next, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we look at the first line there, do you recognise your signature on the first line?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: That, correct me if I'm wrong, please, indicates a dextrose or the commencement of a 10% dextrose infusion. We can
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: see the rate, as we read across, being administered intravenously and that beginning at 03.00, is that, on 17 February?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Thank you. By that time, there was an intravenous line for [Baby K] for that dextrose to be delivered?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Can we then go on, please, to the next tile, tile 38, and look behind that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is, as it says, a blood gas record. We've seen these before. Are they your initials on the right-hand side of the first, I think, two lines in fact?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So we can see there at 03.03 -- is that a venous blood sample --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: -- taken?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And the results across that particular line. So this would, would it, have been shortly after [Baby K]'s arrival in the NNU?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: With the first observation at 02.45 and then the intravenous dextrose and the blood gas record being taken?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The blood gas would have been taken while inserting a cannula. That's why it's a venous sample.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we look next, please, at your nursing note for that first period of time that you spent with [Baby K]. It's at tile 39. To the top left, please, Mr Murphy and the first section of that nursing note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm going to go through it with you, if I may, and if you have anything to add or it reminds you of anything significant, please let me know.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Baby girl born at 25 plus 1 gestation" is your note. This is made at 04.48, so in retrospect once the opportunity arose; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: You've noted there that it was a footling breech delivery which you told us yesterday. "Baby born in fair condition", you describe it, with the caveat to see the medical notes for the full details; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: You've noted that [Baby K] was intubated at approximately 12 minutes of age with a size 2 endotracheal tube, that Curosurf was given. We have heard that's a surfactant; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: She was brought through to the unit and placed in the humidified incubator; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: You've noted her weight at 692 grams. You've noted that you commenced ventilation; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: You told us yesterday a little bit about that. You put the rate, the concentration of oxygen, and you put there that a high leak was noted. Can you tell us what a high leak is, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A high leak is noted on the ventilator, so it gives you a percentage of the leak. It's part of an observation that we do as part of the checks for the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Obviously, if there was any concerns, I would just highlight that to the medical team.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. So is it as the name suggests, air escaping one way or the other?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It sometimes can be with the size of the tube, the ET tube.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Where and in what direction is the air leaking, if that makes sense? Is it leaking on the way into the baby, is it leaking on the way out or both?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know if I'm honest. I don't know if it's an amalgamation of both.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: That's something that the monitors would have detected; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: How would you have detected that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Only on the ventilator itself, the machine.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right. Would the ventilator have an alarm to alert you to that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And would you have raised that with anybody?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, because obviously when we take observations every hour, part of our observation is to note the percentage of leak on the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. Were there any concerns about the leak and its impact on [Baby K]'s ventilation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember at the time. Obviously I would have been highlighting it to the medical staff, but looking at the clinical picture of [Baby K] and her -- if she was stable and ventilating well, the clinical picture with the blood gases.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So is this right, the ventilator is telling you there's a leak? Are you looking elsewhere for the potential impact of that leak?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You're looking at her condition.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right. What was she, as a matter of fact, connected to, a monitor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was she connected to a monitor?
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Would that be the Philips monitor that we have heard about in nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Would that have alerted you to any, for example, drop in saturations?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Or any other impact of that particular problem?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It would -- obviously the monitor is there to pick up heart rate, saturations and respiratory rate, so they would pick up those things if there was a deterioration.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. Now, if [Baby K]'s ventilation over that period had been compromised, would you have been alerted to that by the Philips monitor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, repeat the question?
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: If there'd been any problems with [Baby K]'s ventilation, whether it be the tube or the ventilator itself, would that Phillips alarm have alarmed you to any deterioration in her condition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If clinically she wasn't getting the required ventilation support then, yes, the alarms would go off.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Just describe to us what the -- about the alarms then, please. So you told us that the monitor is reading saturations —
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: -- heart rate -- and what was the third thing you mentioned?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Respiratory rate.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Respiratory rate, okay. So at what point and in what circumstances would an alarm be sounding?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So depending on the parameters that it's set -- it's a preterm infant, so you have two types of alarms. So if the baby desaturated or heart rate dropped, you would be alerted in a softer alarm. But if it fell below that further it would be a more persistent alarm.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Who sets the parameters?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We do.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Would they be standard parameters --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: -- for a baby of that gestation in that condition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. They are set as standard on the Philips monitor on every admission, but as our job on admission or at some point every shift we should be checking what those parameters are and if they are acceptable for that baby.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you happen to remember what they were for [Baby K]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right. Had they fallen below whatever was required, there would have been an alarm?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There would have been, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Initially what you describe as a soft alarm?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And then a more urgent alarm?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right. The soft alarm, just describe what that consists of, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's where if there's a desaturation or a slight decrease in heart rate, that would start to warn you.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: With a red alarm, it's more persistent, like I said, it comes up red and you have it as amber and red.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: What colour is the first alarm?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Amber.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Does it make a noise?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: The second alarm, if it goes even lower, below another threshold, presumably, it's red?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Is the noise the same?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: What's the difference?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's less soft, it's more alerting you.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. Is there a way to disable the alarm on the Philips monitor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, you can acknowledge it, you can pause the alarms.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Are they the same thing or are they two different --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, I apologise, because we now use new upgraded Philips monitors, but in this instance with [Baby K] it would have been an older version. So there is a pause alarm, which you can pause first or you can pause it for a number of minutes if you were doing a procedure or anything.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. So the alarm can be paused, what, in advance of when you know there's going to be a drop in a particular reading or is it only once the alarm's activated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Usually once the alarm is activated.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Is it possible to disable the alarm in advance?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you know, I can't remember on the old ones. You can on the new Philips monitors, but I couldn't be 100% sure.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: You've already told us that it's possible for a nurse to adjust the parameters whereby the alarm does or doesn't sound.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The alarm limits, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you have any recollection of [Baby K]'s breathing being compromised during that first hour that she was in the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not to my recollection, but obviously looking at my notes, it'd just be through my...
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: When you noted the high leak on the ventilator, would you have checked the ventilation at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I would have checked that obviously she's clinically stable --
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and made sure that the tube was still in place.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So would you have inspected the tube and its position?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would have looked at where it was measuring at the lips.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right. Now, I asked you about that hour because there came a point where you went to visit [Baby K]'s parents; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: At what stage did you feel able, if at all, to leave [Baby K] to see her parents?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I feel it's obviously really important to make sure that the family are kept updated, so I wouldn't have left [Baby K] if it wasn't the case that it was stable to do so.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. So would you have satisfied yourself that that was the case?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If I've left then yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: We've heard that when taking over as a designated nurse in the usual way, there would be checks on the equipment and the alarms at the outset of the shift. Would that have been the case during the course of your time with [Baby K] up to then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, but obviously I have gone through for the delivery of [Baby K]. The intensive care spaces should always be checked and they're checked every night.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: As far as you know, did [Baby K] have any issues when you left her to speak to her parents?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Obviously that she was born extremely premature, so...
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Anything beyond that? Any concerns about her condition, her stability, the equipment, anything at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. She was with other -- you know, other members of staff while I went and updated.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So even though, am I right, you satisfied yourself it was appropriate to go, did you still ask someone to keep an eye?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, there will always be someone.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you remember asking anyone in particular?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: When you left [Baby K], can you recall whether she was active or not?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby K] was quite active and that's not uncommon for preterm babies for this stressed period when they've just been delivered, so I do remember her being quite active.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you happen to recall whether at the point you left her she'd had any morphine administered at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not without looking at my notes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right. Well, we'll look at your notes now, but could we first look, so we have a timeline, at the swipe data at 03.47, Mr Murphy? If we can go back to the front of the presentation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we have the benefit of the swipe data. I'm not going to ask Mr Murphy to go behind it, but that's the swipe data that indicates that you left the neonatal unit at 03.47. Is that consistent with your recollection? Does that sound about right for when you went to see [Baby K]'s parents?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Only on recollection of my notes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right. Let's go to the -- I asked you about the morphine. Can we go, please, to tile 50, Mr Murphy? If we can look behind it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is one of the documents that we have in the bundles for the jury, the small paper bundle. I'm happy to distribute them now or just continue with the witness electronically if that's deemed more appropriate. It's a bit difficult zooming in, that's the problem, on some of the entries. So I'm happy to circulate them now.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Speaking for myself I'd like them now if we're going to look at this document.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Divider 14, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Handed)
So jury bundle 2, please, and behind divider 14.
Only two pages for now.

So two pages, the first page being the observation chart we looked at last thing yesterday. If I can ask everyone to turn to the second page, please, which is the neonatal intensive care chart. I'm afraid the copying is very small, so I hope this assists. We can always ask Mr Murphy to zoom in if necessary.
It should be on your screen, Nurse Williams.
Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can I just remind you to keep your voice up, please? I'm told that I'm allowing it to drop and I apologise.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: It's my fault. On the right-hand side, we can see the columns with various entries in from on the form, 01.00, thank you. And we can see that your first entry is 03.30 and under the column which says "Morphine", we can see "commenced". Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So on the face of it, does that suggest that morphine began at 03.30?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to look now, because there's some contradictions within this, which I'm going to ask you, if you can, to explain, please. If we go to the left-hand side of the page, and we look down to the freehand columns at the very bottom, Mr Murphy. They're on their side, unfortunately. So as we look now on the left, your initials are in those first five hourly entries?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And we have, and we can look at the time if we need to -- it says 03.50. Is that 100 micrograms per kilogram of morphine? Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Is that your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Does that relate to a bolus or an infusion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A bolus.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right. So as far as this page is concerned, the infusion began at 03.30 and there was a bolus at 03.50?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: According to those, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: According to the file. I'm going to ask you, please, next to look at a document behind tile 69.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is an infusion chart. Only one entry. If we can look at that, please. We can see the first dose, 17 February 2016, 03.50, which is the time we have just seen for the bolus. But is that a different rate or quantity to that that was recorded as a bolus?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, because it's -- that's an infusion.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right. So according to this document, the infusion began at 03.50?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. It's my signature, but it's not my handwriting. It would have been a doctor who would have prescribed it.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right, okay. If we look up towards the top right, it says "Doctor's signature". Is that likely to be the doctor who filled in the column we're looking at?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And your signature relates to the administration of the infusion rather than any other material; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So you haven't filled that time in at 03.50?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Was that your handwriting on the other chart we looked at where it said "Commenced at 03.30"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On the first side, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Yes, all right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But 03.30 is between that hour and that's where I've written commenced. So it could not be 03.30 exactly, it could be 03.45, 03.40.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. Just knowing the time that you left, at 03.47, you can't assist with whether it was before or after the 03.47?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right. But we know there was a line fitted from at least 3 o'clock because that's when the dextrose began?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Go back to you leaving the unit then, please. When you left the unit, do you recall how [Baby K] was presenting at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, other than, like I said, if she wasn't stable on the ventilator, I wouldn't have left.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: How far, how long to get to where [Baby K]'s parents were?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's next door, the labour ward. I can't remember what room mum was in.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you remember the conversation with her parents?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you remember anything about it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I remember that I would have updated them and given them a treasure box, hopefully a photograph, which is usually what we try and do for every admission.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: A treasure box, is that something that is prepared for the parents at that early stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. They are premade, they're journey boxes to keep mementos in.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Are you able to estimate how long you were with [Baby K]'s parents?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember, I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: How long would that ordinarily take?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Every family's different, every baby's different.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Of course. All right. Did you make your way back to the neonatal unit once you'd spoken to them?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would have thought so.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. And what, if anything, did you find when you got back to the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I remember walking back into the neonatal unit and hearing the alarms sound.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Can you remember whether it was the red or the amber alarm?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Red alarm.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Did you know where that was coming from?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Did you go into nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I would have.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: What did you see?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm so sorry, I'm really struggling to find -- to remember. Obviously, other than my notes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. Do you have any independent recollection of your return to nursery 1 at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Other than that, you know, it seemed like an emergency.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Something was going on and I walked back into it.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you remember how you felt having come back to that situation given what you have told us so far?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, upset, but you do... It's always frightening to go back into a situation like that.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right. Do you remember any conversation with anybody when you got back into that room?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not in the room necessarily, but I did, you know -- Dr Jayaram, who was on, had asked me how this had happened. I thought the ET tube was secure, but I wasn't there, you know.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Let's just approach that. So you remember speaking to Dr Jayaram, but you can't remember who was doing what in nursery 1; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. I think Caroline Oakley and Lucy were there.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you remember when this conversation took place with Dr Jayaram?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, not on the timescale. It wasn't nursery 1. It might have been near the nurses' station.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Tell us, please, then what the thrust of the conversation was.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I just remember him asking me after we'd stabilised [Baby K] again -- I believe we re-intubated... Then just asking how it had happened. Just a very relaxed "How's it happened" question.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Your first recollection with me a moment or two ago was that he mentioned the tube. Do you remember what was said about the tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, just that obviously -- sorry, what do you mean?
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: I don't want to put words in your mouth. When you first told us about the conversation, you told us something he asked about the tube or he made a comment about the tube.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: How did the tube dislodge? How did it move?
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right. I think you also told us, again I don't want to put words in your mouth, the context in which he was asking you that, bearing in mind the evidence you've given to us about before you left [Baby K] on her own.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you recall that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry?
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: You told us that -- you've answered questions about the tube, how secure it was, how it would have been inspected and how it had been secured as far as you were aware.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Doctor, you have come along today to assist us with your care of a baby by the name of [Baby K] --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- and in particular, the early hours of 17 February 2016?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Were you the consultant on duty that particular night?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would have been. I'd have taken over being on call on the day before at around 4 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: With heard that [Baby K] was born at a gestational age of 25 weeks.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And arrived at 02.12 in the morning of 17 February?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Were you on the unit at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would have been called in. So the registrar on call would have called me at home and -- in these situations, with a baby of 25 weeks' gestation, where it is very likely that there are going to be some potentially difficult situations, it would be normal practice for the consultant to actually come in and, if possible, be present at the time of delivery. Sometimes deliveries happen out of the blue and we get there after the time of the delivery, but in this situation I was present at the time that [Baby K] was delivered.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: [Baby K] was 25 weeks' gestation. We've heard about the distinction between secondary and tertiary units, neonatal
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: units. Would a 25-week baby ordinarily be delivered at a secondary unit like Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Ordinarily, no. So until probably the early 2000s, there was less structure about things. But it is recognised that babies below certain gestations, 28 weeks at that time, are better served, if possible, to be born in a tertiary centre. So if it can be anticipated, mothers are transferred to the tertiary centres before a baby is born.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Some situations arise where a mother is already in fairly advanced labour and transfer is not possible because of the risk of a baby actually being born in an ambulance between the secondary and tertiary centres.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So from time to time babies of lower gestations are born in secondary centres and we have the skills and have the ability to manage them in the short term and stabilise them so that they can then be transferred to a tertiary centre.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Was that the case with [Baby K]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely. So in this situation it would have been the obstetricians, who are the team that look after the mothers, who would have made the decision that on balance the risk of transferring at this stage of labour would have been too great and so a decision was made for [Baby K] to be born at the Countess.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Were you present at [Baby K]'s birth?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was present when she was born, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Did you complete notes at [Baby K]'s birth?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I did -- well, retrospectively, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Have you had access to those notes in refreshing your memory for today's purposes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have done, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Can we go to tile 28, Mr Murphy? Your notes are over several pages. I just want to look at the first page, which is behind this tile, first. If you can take us through the note. As you say, dated 17 February and written 04.50 in retrospect as you mentioned a moment ago. You have put there -- is that 25/00?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: 25/40. That means that [Baby K] was born at 25 weeks' gestation, given 40 weeks is the normal gestation. So it's a common notation of gestation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. You have then put "Mum 33 years"; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct and no previous live births and that [Baby K] was an IVF baby.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The next comment, SROM, that means spontaneous rupture of membranes. That means that the amniotic membranes had ruptured over 48 hours before [Baby K] was born. That's important because if there has been a prolonged rupture of membranes, there's a higher risk of infection in a baby because bacteria can cross up into the baby. It doesn't mean the baby necessarily has infection on board, but there's a higher risk and we can anticipate potentially more problems than otherwise.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I also commented that [Baby K]'s mother had received two doses of steroids. When premature delivery can be anticipated, the obstetric and midwifery team administer steroid medication to the mothers of premature babies.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The rationale for doing this is it helps to mature the lungs. The main problem, in terms of lung disease, in very premature babies is absence of a substance called surfactant, which helps to hold the lungs open because the cells that produce surfactant are not present and not working at lower gestations.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Steroids, without going into too much detail, stimulate those cells in the lungs to mature and start producing surfactant. So it doesn't mean that the lungs are going to be fine, but it reduces the potential severity of respiratory distress syndrome, which is the condition caused by surfactant deficiency.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I also make the comment that although the membranes had been ruptured for around 48 hours, there hadn't been any reported temperatures in [Baby K]'s mum and that's relevant as well because maternal temperature also increases the potential risk of infection in a newborn.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Right. Is that "short labour"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Spontaneous labour. "Spont" is short for spontaneous.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And footling, as we have heard, a breech delivery?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Footling breech means --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We have heard. We've been told, thank you, by Dr Smith.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You then noted she was born at 02.12. Is that her weight at 692 grams?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Resuscitated by Dr James Smith?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Is that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He was the registrar on call that night.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Just the next entry on the line, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Initially, when [Baby K] came out, she looked quite dusky.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That's a reference to her colour. Dusky means she looked generally bluish.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: After the word James Smith --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Paed reg", sorry.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Paediatric registrar.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sorry, I imagined something different.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that "no respiratory effort"?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Is that a reading underneath?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A heart rate around 60 beats a minute. The initial assessments we do with any newborn are essentially to give us an idea of what we need to do to help assist the transition from being in utero to being outside. With breech deliveries, particularly footling breech, and she was premature, it can take a little bit longer for babies to be delivered and in that period of time the baby can have less blood flowing through the umbilical cord and can potentially have problems.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So the absence of gasping or respiratory effort is significant. The heart rate being 60 at birth is also significant because we want the heart rate to be above 100. And the fact that she was floppy without great tone and quite pale and dusky coloured is also significant.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So in this situation, we have a pathway that we follow and after initially stimulating and drying the baby, we give what are called inflation breaths.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Inflation breaths essentially simulate what a baby would normally do when they're born. When babies are very first born they take a very big gasp and they have to take a very big gasp because their lungs are full of fluid so the first breath is very difficult. It's analogous to blowing up a balloon: when you first blow up a balloon it's very difficult, you have to put a lot of effort in, but once the balloon is inflated it becomes easier. So a baby take a big gasp.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In this situation, if a baby hasn't gasped, essentially by giving inflation breaths we simulate that. So we give a breath that goes on rather than for a second, for 2 or 3 seconds and we give five breaths.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We do that either with a bag and mask or with a T-piece and mask. What we do when we do inflation breaths is look to see that the chest is moving. When you give one set of inflation breaths, you then reassess. If the chest has moved you know that gas is getting into the lungs. But if the heart rate hasn't picked up we give another round of inflation breaths.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And we see here there were two rounds?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We did two cycles of inflation breaths and then I have said IPPV, which stands for intermittent positive pressure ventilation. And that means, as opposed to inflation breaths, we are giving breaths at a normal rate using the T-piece. And we observe to see that the chest is moving up and down.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If the chest is moving we know that gas is going in and out of the lungs, we know air is going in and out of the lungs. And if that's the case and the heart is beating then what should happen is that as we are oxygenating the lungs, and the heart is pumping blood to the lungs, that blood is getting oxygenated. Oxygenated blood is then coming back to the heart, which then perfuses the heart muscle, which then makes the heart rate pick up. And indeed after 2.5 minutes, [Baby K]'s heart was above 100 beats a minute.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we can scroll down, Mr Murphy. You mentioned the gasps from 3 minutes. Are they gasps that you're looking for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yeah, those are a good sign. Babies should gasp when they come out. The fact that she had a difficult delivery suggests she was a bit stunned. We'd got her heart rate above, we were oxygenating her and she starting gasping at 3 minutes and then breathing spontaneously for herself from 4 minutes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That's the next entry?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Then you have recorded the oxygen saturations at 85% --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Overspeaking) were above (overspeaking) greater than 85% at 6 minutes --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Which --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- (overspeaking) you don't expect oxygen saturations in the first few minutes of life to sit at normal saturations. So that's a good sign -- and in this situation we would have anticipated that she would have had a degree of surfactant deficiency. So sats above 85% at 6 minutes are satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: She's been intubated; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Successfully?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What's the relevance of the 20 minutes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So intubation is a way of getting a more secure airway.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The important thing with management of the airway and breathing at birth is to make sure that we can get air/oxygen in and out of the lungs. Intubation means we have a more secure airway and it enables us to give artificial surfactant.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Intubation is a tricky technique and in smaller babies it can be more difficult. The risk of intubation is that if you spend too long trying to intubate, the baby can have a period where they're not actually breathing or having their breathing done for them. So in the process of intubation in this situation, we make sure that their saturations are as good as they can be, with our hand ventilation, with the mask. We then intubate using a device called a laryngoscope and an endotracheal tube, and we give ourselves 30 seconds to successfully intubate. Somebody independently times 30 seconds and if you don't intubate within 30 seconds we stop the procedure and put the baby back on to the bag and mask or the T-piece and mask and ventilate again.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It took three attempts to intubate [Baby K] and we put -- on the third attempt by Dr Smith we took a decision to put a slightly narrower bore tube in because sometimes in small babies the
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: difficulty can be that you can see the vocal cords and just not pass a tube through.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now, the trouble with a smaller tube -- and we're talking fractions in terms of sizes. This is referring to the internal diameter of the tube of 2 millimetres, ideally at this gestation a 2.5-millimetre tube would have been a better fit but in the circumstances, given intubation was trickier than anticipated, a decision was made to put a size 2 tube in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: This was secured at 6.5 centimetres at the lips.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That means -- if you look at an endotracheal tube, there are markings every centimetre. We intubate through the mouth and the point that the tube emerged from the mouth was 6.5 centimetres.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So the tube is marked in advance with --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is a pre-marked tube, so the tubes actually have markings on.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We can see that [Baby K] was moved to the NNU?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. And while she was being transferred, she would have been being ventilated by hand through the endotracheal tube.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We've heard she would have completed that journey on the Resuscitaire?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And then been transferred to an incubator on arrival in, as it turned out, nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we can scroll down, please. So is this -- it's headed "on arrival". Is this on arrival at nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On arrival at nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So you have recorded the ventilation settings; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Talking through the ventilation settings, I've put 21/5. That means that she had a background pressure, what we call the PEEP, positive end expiratory pressure, of 5 centimetres of water, which is fairly standard in the situation, and a peak pressure of 21, which is the pressure that each breath was being given at. We judge the pressures, really, on
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: what is needed to make sure that we can see the chest moving. So a pressure of 21/5 in a 25-week gestation baby isn't a huge amount of pressure to inflate the lungs. The "T in" of 0.4 is the inspiratory time. So that means each breath we gave was 0.4, and normally 0.4 to 0.5 seconds is what we would do.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And she was needing around 60% oxygen through the ventilator circuit. I've commented there that on these settings her chest was moving well and when I listened she had good air entry. That means with a stethoscope I could hear gas going in and out of lungs, I could hear air moving in and out of her lungs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: She had an initial gas, which is a venous gas -- so venous gases always have a slightly lower pH than an arterial or capillary gas. Her pH was 7.23. Her PCO2, which is the amount of carbon dioxide in her blood, the waste product of breathing, was 7. In babies we often accept slightly higher CO2s and slightly lower pHs at this stage, particularly with a venous gas, because we know that trying to ventilate to normality can potentially cause harm to the lungs. So we call it permissive hypercapnia and we are happy to let them have a little bit of leeway with their carbon dioxide.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Her bicarbonate was 23, which is a reflection of the metabolic side of things, which is normal. Her lactate was a little bit high at 4, which was not a surprise given that she'd had a little bit of a difficult birth.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: She was given surfactant down the endotracheal tube at 2.45. And following this, her oxygen requirement came down slightly to 50%.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: For fluids, we can see "IV access obtained"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She'd have had a cannula placed.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Is that BM?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: BM is a term for blood glucose. It's a bit like calling a vacuum cleaner a hoover. BM was the original machine that did it. So a blood glucose of 4, which again is acceptable and perfectly good for this age.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We commenced her, as we would have done standardly, on a 10% dextrose infusion at 60ml per kilogram of body weight per day, which is the standard formula for fluids in newborns.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I've commented that we sent a blood culture off.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The reason for this is because there were risk factors for infection. So spontaneous premature delivery in itself can
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: happen because of infection and there was a history of a prolonged rupture of membranes and she had significant respiratory symptoms. Even though that was likely to be due to surfactant deficiency, we can't exclude infection, so it was important to make the assumption until proven otherwise that infection was present and we do this routinely. So we sent a blood culture off. A blood culture is a blood test to see down the line if any bacteria are growing in the bloodstream. But rather than waiting for that result we assume it is there until we know it is not and she was commenced on two intravenous antibiotics, penicillin and gentamicin.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we scroll down we can see the meds she was administered. Is that vitamin K?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, she received intramuscular vitamin K. Again, newborn babies get this as matter of routine to reduce the risk of a condition called haemorrhagic disease of the newborn, which can happen because babies' clotting factors are not entirely mature.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: As I mentioned she was started on penicillin and gentamicin -and with ventilated babies we usually start them on medication as (sic) analgesia and sedation. And that's why she was started on morphine because it's not pleasant to have a plastic tube going down into your airway. So as a matter or routine we want to keep these babies as comfortable as possible and 20 micrograms per kilogram per hour is a fairly standard starting dose for a morphine infusion in a newborn baby -- or indeed an older child as well.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you recall at what stage of [Baby K]'s introduction to the nursery the morphine was commenced?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't recall exactly when. I don't recall. It's not usually straightaway because it takes time to
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: (inaudible: coughing) it up and draw it up as well.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm sorry, I can't read the --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The rest are just examination findings. I commented on initial assessment at that time that her -- she was pink in colour, having been dusky. She had good tone, having been floppy previously. Her pulses were of good volume and easy to feel. Her capillary refill -- that's when we push over the sternum for 5 seconds and take our finger away and the colour should come back in less than 2 seconds. That's a sign that, from a circulation point of view, we are in a good place.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And that line with (inaudible) is a way of documenting that her heart sounds were normal. So I could hear her two heartbeats, I couldn't hear any extra sounds such as murmurs. I have written there that her chest was moving equally on both sides and when I listened to her lung fields I could hear air going or gas going in and out of her lungs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to pause there. [Baby K] is being moved from the delivery suite to nursery 1. You told us about the ventilation settings. And we've heard from her designated nurse how she would be connected to the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: At this stage, bearing in mind the note you just told us, do you have any observations about the efficiency of ventilation or otherwise?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, the fact that the chest was moving and I could hear air going in and out of the lungs and the oxygen saturations, which I haven't documented there, were acceptable in the amount of oxygen she was in. For a 25-week gestation baby I was happy with where she was.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Obviously, we are always aware that over time surfactant deficiency can cause worsening symptoms. So she would need to be watched closely in terms of her chest movement, in terms of her oxygen requirement, in terms of her blood gases.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Were you satisfied at that stage that the ventilation was working properly?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I was. The reason I say that is, as I say, I could see her chest moving and air was going in and out of her lungs. Remember, the purpose of what we're trying to do with the ventilator is to get gas in and out of the lungs and if the chest is moving and we can hear gas going in and out of the lungs, then we know -- we are working out: is it enough, is it too much? We have to look at what her oxygen saturations are doing, we have to have a look at blood gases as well.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Erm --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But I certainly wasn't concerned at this stage that we needed to change a huge amount acutely because, as I say, her chest was moving and she was a good colour.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And you've noted her -- is that "abdo soft"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Her tummy was soft, so she didn't have an obviously distended tummy. Sometimes, when we've been ventilating with a
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: mask, gas, as well as going into the lungs, can go into the abdomen and sometimes the tummy can get distended. But her tummy was very soft and I commented that she had good tone neurologically.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So at this point I spoke with the neonatal transport team. So we have a team who transfer babies between units and they're a very specialised, highly trained team and they have the equipment and the ambulance equipment to come to us, pick up babies, and transfer them to the tertiary centres. And as I said earlier, ideally it is better for these babies to be born in tertiary centres, but it doesn't happen uncommonly at all that babies can't be transferred or babies come in and are born in the secondary centres. And they advised there was a bed at Arrowe Park, a cot at Arrowe Park Hospital, and they asked us if we could, whilst we were waiting for them, try and place umbilical lines and get some X-rays done.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And I've commented at that point I updated [Baby K]'s parents. I don't remember what I said or doing that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I would have gone back to the labour ward to update them, just really to tell them where we were and what the plan was.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to ask, please, to put a note that you made — did you prepare a plan for the police to show where [Baby K] was in the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have a recollection I did, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you put that up, please, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The delivery suite is over to the right. [Baby K] was where the A is circled.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Where we have neonatal unit, we know that the map is inaccurate to the extent there's a door above the O or the N here.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It's been missed off the plan.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That's nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And as far as you're concerned on the map, your A is where [Baby K] was placed in nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We'll come back to that in a moment please. Were you aware, having seen [Baby K] in nursery 1, who her designated nurse was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was Jo Williams.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Were you aware at any point that Joanne Williams left the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So we were happy that [Baby K] was stable. We didn't have to particularly change her ventilator settings a huge amount, her chest was moving, she was settled, she had her antibiotics, she was on a morphine infusion and she was very, very settled.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Jo Williams told me -- and I don't know if you want to go back to that picture because I can tell you where I was.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I will ask you a question first.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, of course.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You've given us a summary of [Baby K]'s condition at that point and you were content that she was settled. You mentioned that the morphine infusion had started?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Overspeaking).
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I want you to look, please, at tile 69.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is the infusion chart, which reflects the morphine infusion that we understand [Baby K] received.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That does state it started at 03.50.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes. So we can see there, the date, the time, the rate; can you see your signature?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can see my signature, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Are those details in your hand?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's my writing, yes, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So that would have been the infusion, the time that you understand the infusion to have started?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Looking at that, yes, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: When Nurse Williams left -- do you recall her leaving?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. She came to me and she said she was going to go to the labour ward to update [Baby K]'s parents.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Were you aware that she went?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Where did you go?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was sitting at the desk, which is just round the corner from the other door on -- in nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Let's go back to the plan, please. The cursor should work, I hope. On the mouse to the left of the screen --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I was (indicating) there.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Tell us what's there, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There are some shelves there and there's a desk here with drawers underneath it and a chair.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you recall what you were doing at the desk?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was either writing a note or waiting for the transfer team to come back, but I recall I was writing a note.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I don't know whether it was [Baby K]'s notes or other notes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What, if anything, happened at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So Jo had told me that she was going to the labour ward to update [Baby K]'s parents and she told me that Lucy Letby was -- we use the word babysitting -- was going to keep an eye on things.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'll talk you through my thought processes. Now, at this point in the February, we were aware, as a team, of a number of unexpected, unusual events, and we were aware of the association with Lucy Letby being there.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That's all we were aware of. Nothing else had been -- no cause/effect had been ascribed. I will admit, it seems entirely illogical and irrational, but when Jo told me she was going and Lucy was there, I felt extremely uncomfortable.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now, you can call me hysterical, you can call me irrational, but that's how I felt because of this association. And then the
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: rational part of myself told me to stop being ridiculous and I carried on doing what I was doing. And this thought recurrently came into my head. So after about 2 or 2.5 minutes, I got up and went to walk up, just to check on [Baby K]. And the reason I did that was actually to prove to myself that I needed to stop being ridiculous and irrational and, of course, everything was going to be okay and then I could go back and just carry on with doing what I was doing. And I would say it was probably 2.5 to 3 minutes, I think, after Jo had told me that she was going to the labour ward from my recollection.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So I got up. I had not heard -- I'd not been called to come to review [Baby K] and I'd not got up because I'd heard alarms going off and -- an alarm going off in nursery 1 -- and I don't recall there were any other babies in nursery 1, although I may be wrong. I would have heard an alarm. So I got up and walked through to see [Baby K].
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. Did you go into nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I went into nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you remember which door you used to go into nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I went in through the door that isn't on the drawing
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So the door nearest the desk?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and I walked through and walked up.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. What, if anything, did you see when you went into nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So, as I walked up, I saw Lucy Letby standing by the ventilator by the incubator. She didn't have her hands in the incubator, and I saw her, and then I looked up at the monitor. And on the monitor [Baby K]'s saturations were dropping. So her saturations are a reflection of her oxygenation. And when I got there, they were in the 80s and they continued to drop.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The ventilator wasn't alarming and the monitor wasn't alarming. The monitors are set to alarm usually when the saturations drop below 90%. I recall saying,
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: "What's happening?", and Lucy looked and said words along the lines of, "She's having a desaturation". And at that point, the important thing is to then assess the baby and try to work out why that desaturation is happening.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Let's just pause there. We've got a map in front of us.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is there any significance in the B that you have marked
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I recall that might have been -- if A is the incubator, that was where Lucy Letby was standing.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And before we move on to your conversation, you told us she was standing near to the incubator?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, right at the top. So the incubator is obviously where A is. The ventilator machine is here
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: (indicating), the monitor is above here (indicating), and there's various infusion pumps and she was standing at the top end of the incubator, as close -- the ventilator would have been sitting where the cursor is there, so she was standing there (indicating).
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Which way would [Baby K] have been lying in the --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby K]'s head was towards the wall and feet towards the other end.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Right. So she was standing alongside the incubator?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What, if anything, was she doing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nothing. She hadn't actually -- I wasn't aware that she was looking at the monitor. She was facing -- I can't remember, she wasn't facing away from me, she was facing more towards me but didn't actually say anything to me until I asked her what's happening.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you remember where you were in the room when you first spoke to her?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Probably as I was walking -- probably about halfway because I'd walked in and it was at this point that I had looked up and seen that the saturations were dropping.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You told us the priority was the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What did you do?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In this situation, if a baby is -- if a ventilated baby is desaturating again there's a number of things we have to think about as to why this baby is desaturating. So the first thing is to look at the baby because it might just be that the monitor is not picking up properly and the baby is fine. But when I looked at her, you could see that the chest, which had been moving with the breaths from the ventilator, was no longer moving. So immediately, if the chest isn't moving one has to think, why isn't the chest moving, is there a problem with ventilator tube, is there a problem with the lungs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The first thing then is to look at the ventilator and the ventilator was still delivering breaths. When you look at the chest, it's not moving, you listen to the chest and can't hear air moving in and out, that suggests then there's some kind of issue with the tube but it could be an issue with the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So I disconnected the ventilator from the endotracheal tube, and put a T-piece on with a thing called a CO2 monitor. A CO2 monitor is a device that -- if carbon dioxide, the waste product of breathing, is coming out of the lungs, the CO2 monitor will change colour.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I gave breaths through the T-piece with the CO2 monitor on through the endotracheal tube. Two observations: the chest didn't move and the CO2 monitor didn't change. That suggests that the tube is not functioning as it should be. That will either be because it's not in the right place, it's become dislodged, or it's happening because it's blocked in some way.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It could also be happening because the lung disease, which -- we know surfactant-deficient lung disease/respiratory distress syndrome evolves over time and it could have deteriorated to the point where the lungs were so stiff that we couldn't give enough pressure to inflate the lungs. But I felt that was unlikely given that a few minutes before, on the ventilator settings we were on, we were stable.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Pausing there, was there any more conversation between the two of you as you did this?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We switch into professional mode and say, look, we have to deal with this situation. So I may have asked,
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: "What's happened?", because it didn't really make sense to me why the tube should become dislodged because it was secured, it was in at 6.5 centimetres at the lips, and [Baby K] wasn't a vigorous baby, she had good tone.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It's very difficult to dislodge an ET tube without it being spotted. So it can happen if a baby is having cares and being handled. It can happen if a baby is very vigorous and their hand gets caught under the tube and they pull it. But [Baby K] wasn't really behaving like that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So I then removed the tube, which wasn't blocked, and then put a face mask on the end of the T-piece to ventilate [Baby K]. And as soon as we ventilated through the face mask, [Baby K]'s chest began to move up and down, without a huge amount of difficulty and her saturations picked up.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Did Lucy Letby say anything during the course of that procedure?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nothing that I remember. Nothing that I remember.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I was probably asking her to bring me things and help, but I don't remember any kind of conversation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. So you managed to, through the Neopuff, provide air; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What happened next?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Through the Neopuff with a mask, [Baby K]'s chest moved, her saturations picked up, and that suggested to me that her lungs disease at that point hadn't significantly worsened. Then she was re-intubated.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Did you remove the original tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that was taken out before we -- the sequence was, having disconnected from the ventilator, we ventilated through the original tube with the CO2 monitor. It was clear the chest wasn't moving, it was clear the CO2 monitor wasn't changing colour, so we removed the tube, ventilated with the mask, and then electively re-intubated her, which I believe James Smith did under my supervision.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Bearing in mind the alternatives that you ran through, did you check the tube that was (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it wasn't blocked -- and actually there would have been no reason at this stage for a tube to have been significantly blocked.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: He had actually said that. Dr Jayaram already said, "I removed the tube and it wasn't blocked".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I just wanted to confirm. I missed that.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay, so just talk us through the next phase then, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So James Smith re-intubated and because we were in a more controlled situation, we had more time and we put a size 2.5 tube down, which we would have liked to have done to start with, and she was reconnected to the ventilator. She was on pretty much similar ventilator settings to what she was before this event, which again suggested that whatever had caused that deterioration, it probably wasn't related to a significant worsening in that time of her underlying lung disease.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. How was [Baby K] behaving at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was behaving as I would expect a 25-week gestation baby to behave. She was not really moving a huge amount, but she had normal tone, she wasn't floppy, the intubation was controlled, she stayed pink with good saturations throughout.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So Dr Smith intubated for a second time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He intubated, yes. I can't remember whether he -- how many attempts he took this time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Perhaps if we go to your note, it will assist. If we can go to tile 65, please. It's towards the bottom of the page that we've already been through and continues on to the next.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The other thing I did is check there wasn't a pneumothorax with a cold light and there wasn't a pneumothorax. Again, just thinking through causes for acute deterioration.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So looking for causes eliminating those that you could at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It's important to look for important causes that can be -- that need to be found and treated immediately.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So at 03.50 you described it as a sudden deterioration; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And you have put that the O2 sats dropped to -- is that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Less than 40. So as I say, when I walked into the room they were dropping, they were in the 80s and they started going down.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And at what stage did they reach 40%?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That was before we took the tube out and bagged her back up with the mask.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You then have entered:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Bagged via ET tube with Neopuff."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: "CO2 monitor not changing colour" --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- "and poor chest movement?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- which again indicated to me that we needed to remove the tube.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. The cold light, which we've heard about, was normal in appearance, so not determinative --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, which suggested there was (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- (overspeaking) no sign of --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No sign of a pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Scroll down, please:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Tube removed and bagged via face mask." And you say the sats recovered quickly?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: "Re-intubated by Dr Smith after a bolus of morphine."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, we do that as a matter of routine when we're intubating electively, again more for sedation and comfort for the baby. It makes the intubation process a little easier as well.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the tube was placed, again, at 6.5 centimetres at the lips, so it was the same length in terms of how far in it was as the original tube. And then we listened to both sides and again could hear good air entry and she was put back on to the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And is that ventilation settings (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As previously, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. We can see the change in size of the ET tube from 2 to 2.5. Might that have been a feature in what you saw?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't think so. The reason I say that is that although it is -- we'd have liked to have got a 2.5 in and the fact that there was a size 2 in didn't have any impact on the ventilation. So don't forget the outcome of ventilating is to try to get our gas mixture in and out of the lungs and get oxygen in and carbon dioxide out. If we're in a situation where we were struggling -- so in the period leading up to this deterioration if we'd been having to put the ventilator settings higher and higher to get the chest moving and we were struggling to oxygenate, then it would have been entirely appropriate at that point to say, look, we probably need to try and change to a bigger tube.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: As it was, with the narrower bore tube, we were ventilating effectively, and I don't think that having that narrower bore tube had an impact on her ventilation and I don't believe that had an impact on the event of her sudden deterioration at that time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. I'll come to your plan in a moment. If we scroll up we can see you have timed the event at 03.50.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have written that there, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we go up to that, please. Are you able to assist with how long Nurse Joanne Williams had been away at the time that you went into the nursery?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I honestly can't remember. I can't remember whether Jo Williams was back at the time we re-intubated or not.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. The other question is we looked at an infusion prescription earlier suggesting --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was 03.50.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes, it was 03.50. So can you explain that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would imagine that that's probably when the morphine was prescribed and set up, which is -- it goes against my recollection. I thought it was earlier.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's go then to your plan, please. Your plan was to await line placement, then contact the transport team?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the transport team had already been contacted.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: They'd said, call us back when you've got lines in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: [Baby K]'s parents came to visit [Baby K] on the unit and I updated them as to where we were up to.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So in the aftermath of the incident at 03.50, you've noted that the transport team were already aware of what [Baby K]'s position was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I don't think... I don't think I had updated them at this point of this event that had happened.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Are you able to say when you first contacted them; do you remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Some time between... It would have been before I wrote this because it says:
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: "Await line placement and then contact transport team." If we can go further back, I think I mentioned the transport team earlier on. So I think I'd discussed, before this deterioration at 3.50, looking at the sequence of things, and they'd suggested that we should do some lines and then call them back and they'd come down.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Are they the UVC and UAC that we've heard about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And if I can conclude your plan at this stage. The parents have visited baby on unit and have been updated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: All right. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, is that a convenient moment?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram, we break off for an hour for lunch, so could you please be ready to continue at 2 o'clock? Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Members of the jury, 2 o'clock for you, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Just looking at the witness list for the rest of today, in particular Dr Babarao, I'm not anxious on having that doctor waiting here and not being called.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He cannot come tomorrow, so we'll have to complete him this afternoon. So we were thinking of, at this stage, sending away [Nurse B].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly one of them, I think, should be.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't know how long Mr Myers is going to be.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Maybe about 20 or 25 minutes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Oh right. Well, anyway. I'll leave it to you to discuss. If the witness can't be here tomorrow, that witness should be completed today.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'd reached that view.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The short adjournment)
(In the presence of the jury)
Dr Jayaram, helpfully on the screen is the point we left off at, which was your plan for [Baby K], which speaks of, as you clarified for us, the UVC and the UAC that were planned.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Could I ask Mr Murphy to go to tile 106 next, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can we scroll down, please? We should scroll up maybe.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There are a number of pages on here. There we go, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Where we left off with your plan, an entry from somebody else, from the handwriting, about Curosurf.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then is that your note continuing (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's my handwriting, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. I think we can see -- what's the first line, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have documented that Dr Smith put an umbilical venous catheter in. "9 centimetres at the cord" means that it was inserted to a 9-centimetre length at the umbilical cord. But he was unable to pass a catheter for an umbilical arterial catheter. And we did a chest X-ray to look at the position of the UVC and also to look at the lungs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. We've seen that the X-ray taken -- of course Dr Smith has given evidence already -- was at 6.07 am, so if we can continue with your note at 6.15, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At 6.15 it was noted that [Baby K]'s saturations began to drop and that the tidal volume being measured by the ventilator had dropped a little bit as well. So in this situation, that suggests again there's some kind of issue with the ventilation. This could be an issue with the lungs, it could be an issue with the tube, it could be an issue with the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we scroll down, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But the crucial thing here isn't so much what the ventilator is saying about the tidal volume, it's the fact that the clinical problem was that the saturations were dropping.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the capillary gas there suggests a respiratory acidosis. So the pH of 7.07 is significantly low. The base excess of minus 3 suggests that the metabolic component of it, which is the part of the -- the contribution to the acidosis of the circulation potentially being compromised was probably okay. But the carbon dioxide was 12.8. So this suggests that at that moment, with that deterioration, we had a situation where saturations were dropping and the CO2 was increasing, suggesting we probably had an issue with ventilation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The other thing that was noted was that [Baby K]'s mean blood pressure, so average blood pressure, was 20 millimetres of mercury. Generally, it's difficult to know exactly what a normal blood pressure is, but generally for a mean blood pressure around gestational age is about acceptable. So a mean blood pressure of 25 millimetres of mercury would probably have been okay, but that has to be put in the context of the clinical situation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So there were two things here potentially happening.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM
