blocks.text: There was clearly an issue with ventilation in terms of getting gas in and out of the lungs. But also with oxygenation because the saturations were low. That could have been related to ventilation, but with a low blood pressure, a low body systemic blood pressure, there is a situation that can arise where blood preferentially bypasses the lungs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: To explain this further, there are connections within the heart and outside the heart between the right side of the heart and the left side of the heart that are present when a baby is on the inside, but that usually close when a baby is on the outside. They serve a purpose when a baby's on the inside because the baby gets their oxygen from their mother not through their lungs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In a situation where there is potential difficulty with the lungs being stiff or harder to ventilate, and a low body blood pressure, then actually fluid in pipes takes the path of least resistance and it is easier for blood coming back to the right side of the heart to go through the hole between the atria, the top pumping chambers of the heart, and a thing called the duct, which connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta. And that is the situation in neonatology we call persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So the important thing if the blood pressure is low is try to do things to improve the blood pressure, hence the bolus of normal saline was given. This -- in spite of this, however, the saturations remained low.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We then wondered whether the tube, the endotracheal tube, could have been in the wrong position, could it potentially have slipped down. So we pulled it back, but the saturations dropped and so we extubated.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Again, [Baby K] responded to hand ventilation with a mask. And again, a new endotracheal tube was put in, and she went back on to the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We can see that that was again a 2.5 size ETT.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The same size tube as had been put in when she was reintubated.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And to the same depth of 6.5 centimetres?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And you have noted that she was settled for about the next 30 minutes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then you have another note at 07.25.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, then again her blood pressure dropped. So we gave a further bolus of fluid to try and improve her blood pressure and her saturations picked up and then her saturations and heart rate dropped. Her saturations dropped and her heart rate went below 100 --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we can scroll down. Again, just take your time as we go through the note, please, because it's being transcribed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sure. So we took her off the ventilator and ventilated her with the T-piece through the Neopuff down the endotracheal tube. Cardiac compressions were started not because her heart had stopped but with a heart rate below 100, we can't be sure that enough blood is being pumped around the body, so we assist by starting cardiac compressions. This helps also to bring oxygenated blood back to the heart as well. We noted at this point that the endotracheal tube that had been at 6.5 centimetres now appeared to be at 8 centimetres at the lips --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to pause there. We've got the entry, previous entry, where it's been pulled out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. Then is this the second time it has been pulled out during the course of that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So higher up -- we didn't -- sorry, can you scroll back up again --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Of course.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- to the top of the page, just to talk through the sequence.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So when she had the deterioration prior to this one documented at 7.25, because she wasn't responding, I wondered was the tube too long. We pulled it back to 6 centimetres, but actually she deteriorated. It may be that it had become too short but it wasn't working so we took it out, bagged her, by which I mean ventilated her through the T-piece, and then re-intubated. And then she was settled again.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So this episode at 7.25 was with the tube that was put in at that episode and we noted during this episode that the tube, having been at 6.5 at the lips, was at 8 centimetres at the lips.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Just allow me to correct myself. It's gone in
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's gone in further rather than coming out. And when you see this, a tube should be sitting in the trachea, which is the main pipe, before the trachea divides into the two bronchi. If a tube slips and is too long it can go down into one of the bronchus -- bronchi, usually the right side, because the way the anatomy is, the right lung tube, the right bronchus, is more vertical and it tends to go down that way.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So we withdrew the tube back to 6.5 centimetres and she picked up quite quickly. So I think at that point part of the problem might have been the tube having slipped. And then she settled again.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Is that last entry "now stable"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, "Now stable". And at the time I documented, these were her ventilator settings. Again, pressures of 23/5 --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to interrupt you. We've got them there and if anyone wants to ask you about them in any more detail, I am sure they will. But they represent the settings post that second incident that morning, if I can put it that way -- of course, the earlier incident was in the morning --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- but the one you have just described? We can see the fluids, the meds, set out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we go down to results, the CRP is less than 1.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Lines -- can we go down a little more, please, Mr Murphy? We can see, is that a peripheral --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A peripheral line in her right arm, so a short venous cannula, and the umbilical venous cannula.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. The blood pressure mean has risen a little, you told us before --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It has, to 25.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- to 25. It should be about the gestation period?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's about the minimum that we would be comfortable with.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And the cap refill is satisfactory?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What's the last --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A heart rate of 130. And the other thing just to observe here when -- in the entry for medications, we commenced or planned to commence, I'm not sure what time it was started, a medication called dopamine. So dopamine is from a group of drugs called inotropes which help cardiac contractility, so this was in response to the persistently low blood pressure. And the aim of dopamine in this situation is to try to make the heart beat more strongly, essentially to improve the cardiac output and help to maintain the blood pressure.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. If we can scroll down a little further, please, Mr Murphy. Is that the end of that page? We need 123 then, I think, next.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the end of that clinical entry. I looked at the chest X-ray which had been done before that deterioration and on the chest X-the tube was in a good position, a satisfactory position, and I commented that the left lung field appeared a bit hazier than the one on the right. And then the transport team arrived at 8.30, I have put Anand from the transport team from Arrowe Park and you can see there, after discussion, he added in another inotropic drug in addition to the dopamine to help with cardiac contractility. He suggested a second dose of surfactant and increased the fluid volume as well and suggested, because there was difficulty putting an umbilical arterial catheter in, we should put in a peripheral arterial line.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And really I think from that point, the transport team led on management. I can't remember whether that morning I was there subsequently or whether I handed over to somebody else and went elsewhere to do what I was doing during the day.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Just scroll to the bottom of the page. We might be able to see who else makes an entry. It looks like -- well, we'll hear, or I think it's agreed, it's [Dr A].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and he put that peripheral arterial line in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: At the time he put that in and it was measured through that, the blood pressure, the mean blood pressure was 27 millimetres of mercury.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Just some specific questions now, please, Dr Jayaram.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You were asked about the significance of the size 2 tube in comparison to the size 2.5 and the event at 3.50. What can you tell us about that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So coming back to that, so ideally, it would have been nice to have a 2.5 millimetre internal diameter tube in, but we've put the 2 in because of the difficulties and the time it was taking at the initial resuscitation after birth.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: When we look at observations, the ventilator is quite a clever machine and it can measure lots of things. It can measure, obviously, how much gas goes in and how much gas goes out. Ultimately, what we're trying to do with ventilation, as I've said before, is to get gas in and out of the lungs, to oxygenate the baby, and to be able for the baby to get rid of carbon dioxide.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So a size 2 tube in itself is not a problem. It's only a problem if we're really struggling to ventilate the baby through it. The ventilator will give us all sorts of measurements and one of the things it measures is what's called the leak. If you imagine the baby's top of the baby's windpipe, the larynx, and the tube sits in it, the ventilator can measure how much gas is leaking out around the edges. Now, we want to have some degree of leak, because if there's no leak, it's potentially that the tube is too tight and it can potentially cause damage.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The leak is a calculated value. The ventilator looks at how much gas is put in and how much --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Take your time again, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry. The ventilator measures how much gas goes in down the tube and measures how much gas comes out of the tube and it calculates the leak by the difference between those volumes. Now, a leak in itself is not of any clinical significance because what's important is are we ventilating the baby. So if a leak is a high leak, it's noted, but actually if there's no difficulties with ventilation, we wouldn't act on just a leak.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If a leak was high and we were struggling to ventilate the baby, then it's important then to think, well, is this a problem because we are not able to get enough gas in and out through this narrower tube, we should put a bigger one in --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to pause there. The high leak was noted at a time before Joanne Williams went to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- notify the parents. Would the high leak have caused, if it's what happened, the intubation tube to dislodge?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Would the size of the tube have caused the intubation tube to dislodge?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. I mean, we're talking half a millimetre difference.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. We touched very briefly on the X-ray being at 6.07 and you have told us before that when a baby is intubated, it can be important to take an X-ray --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- to check the position. There's a reason why an X-ray wasn't taken straightaway with [Baby K]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We don't usually do X-rays in this situation until a baby's around 4 hours old because if we're trying to establish whether there's surfactant-deficient lung disease, we won't see the changes until around they are 4 hours old. If we were having difficulties with ventilation or when we looked at the chest, it wasn't moving as it should, or when we listen to the chest there was unequal air entry on both sides, we would consider getting an X-ray earlier. In this situation we were happy with the original intubation, that there was equal air entry when listening with a stethoscope and the chest movement was symmetrical and we were happy that we were adequately ventilating her. So there wasn't an indication to do an earlier chest X-ray.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We would also do an X-ray if we had put an umbilical venous catheter in or an umbilical arterial catheter in, again to check the position. So essentially with investigations we would do them if we think we're going to find something that might change management at that time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. But not in this case?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not at that situation at that time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Again, just concentrating on that period between [Baby K] being intubated and Nurse Williams leaving the neonatal unit, were there any warning signs about the desaturation you were about to witness?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. No, and had there been at the time that Nurse Williams left and told me she was going to the labour ward, I believe absolutely she would have spotted this and told me. So at the time she left, there were no concerns that there was anything to suggest any deterioration.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Bearing in mind the desaturation you witnessed, would [Baby K]'s lung disease explain what you saw?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not at that time because the way that surfactantdeficient lung disease/respiratory distress syndrome gets worse is it evolves. Over time you'll see an increase in ventilatory requirements, you will see an increase in oxygen requirements, you will see blood gases showing more of a respiratory acidosis. But certainly it would be -- one wouldn't expect [Baby K]'s lung disease to have deteriorated in that short period of time from Nurse Williams going to the labour ward to talk to [Baby K]'s parents and me walking into the room.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Did you form a view about how long [Baby K] would have been in the condition she was in when you entered the nursery?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So when babies are reasonably well oxygenated, let's say a point comes where ventilation fails for whatever reason, usually babies will maintain saturations for 30 to 60 seconds before they start desaturating. So for her saturations to have been in the 80s and dropping, my inference is that this would have happened at least -- something would have happened at least 30 to 60 seconds before I walked in. She might have desaturated more quickly because she had RDS, but at the point that Jo Williams left, her saturations were stable.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Were there any calls for assistance before you --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I didn't hear anything. As I say, I explained my rationale and thought processes for going in really just to prove to myself that everything was okay so I could carry on doing what I was doing. I hadn't heard a ventilator alarm or monitor alarm going off and I hadn't been called to say that she was desaturating.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you, doctor. If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
You were worried, Dr Jayaram, given your suspicions you were being irrational, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I was certainly concerned because my logical mind would have said, she's stable, there's nothing to worry about.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: However, having been party to and heard about a number of unusual events by this stage, I was concerned.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So if what you say is correct, what you have told us all things were like when you walked into that nursery, it turns out you weren't being irrational at all?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In the sense that I really didn't want to walk in and find her in anything other than the condition she'd been in when Jo had left. But my reasons for walking in were not based on any clinical suspicion of [Baby K], although she was a premature baby, being at risk of an acute deterioration due to her underlying medical issues.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What you tell us you saw with Lucy Letby and what she was not doing goes to show, if you are right, that you were not being irrational in your concern?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In retrospect no, which I guess is part of why we are here now.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Because, according to you, the woman and you one or more of your colleagues had decided was linked to an increase in incidents since June 2015 was there in highly suspicious circumstances, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You mean, can you elaborate what you mean by she was there in highly suspicious circumstances?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You have described the scene to us; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But it wasn't suspicious that she was there. She was a nurse, she was asked to look after the baby.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You told the police that you thought this might have been done on purpose.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's certainly one of the things that crossed my mind.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That sounds pretty suspicious, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That does, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes. So you're telling us the woman who had been identified by you and one or more of your colleagues as linked in some way to an increase in incidents was standing there in suspicious circumstances?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In that context, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes. You'd got her then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, because I didn't see her do anything, and actually, if I may say at this point, and you have made reference to this before about myself and my colleagues, we had noticed this association and more and more of these events were happening and we really wanted to be able to have this investigated objectively in an appropriate way. And we, at that time, were really unclear as to how we could get this investigated in an appropriate way.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because there was absolutely no... no evidence that we could prove anything, because that's not our job as doctors. Our job is to notice patterns and raise concerns.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You agree, you did tell the police that, confronted with what you saw, you wondered if the tube had been dislodged on purpose?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did wonder that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And you have said to us now how this would have gone on for a certain period of time for the desaturation to reach this point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So did you confront her?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely not. It's my job at the time to deal with the baby, it's not my job to say that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: This is someone who you're saying by this time you have linked to incidents on this department; yes? That's what you're telling us?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It's someone you're saying is standing there when you walked in because of your suspicions; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It is someone who is standing there having done something that you told the police could have been done on purpose?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a possibility.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If it happened the way you are describing it to us, you'd have asked her what was happening?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I wouldn't.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And the reason you didn't ask her is because it didn't happen in the way you're telling us or rather told the police later?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. Well, I'm interested in why you say that because what I have told you and what has been said is exactly my recollection of things.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do we see anywhere in your note, clinical note, anything relating to suspicious circumstances of a dislodged tube?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, Mr Myers, that is not the sort of thing that one writes in clinical notes. It is, however, one of the things that we discussed as a team together, and added to the list of concerns that we already had, and escalated to senior management in the hospital.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In fact, there's no reference to dislodgement of a tube at all in the note, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it's implicit that the tube wasn't in. You can -you can -- from the fact that the tube when we ventilated down it through (sic) hand, there was no change in the CO2, the chest wasn't moving, the tube -- and the tube wasn't blocked. The only reason that tube could not have been working was that it was not in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You don't make reference to any dislodgement because there was nothing suspicious at the time in your mind about a dislodgement, was there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There was a lot suspicious in mind because I still don't understand how a tube could have been dislodged.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We don't in fact see a Datix report about this, do we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't put a Datix in, no.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: A Datix is a standard form that's completed when something has happened that isn't right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We often do them, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And this is more than just not right if you're telling us accurately, isn't it, Dr Jayaram?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's unusual.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Unusual. You're saying it's suspicious and potentially deliberate?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Potentially, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Deliberate harm by someone that you and your colleagues suspect of being associated with a series of events since June 2015, if you're right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And you don't even put a Datix report in, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I wasn't convinced that the Datix system was the correct way to investigate this because this event and any of these events in isolation would have been, hmm, not sure why that happened, and not thought about it. But in the context of the pattern they were more significant and we, as a group of consultants -- and this isn't just me or one or two colleagues, we as a group of consultants by this stage, most of us had had experience of an unusual and unexpected event and had noticed this association with one particular nurse. Now that is by no means us ascribing any kind of guilt, but we were very concerned because not only was there the association with Nurse Letby, but all of these events were unusual.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And yes, if we'd put Datix forms in for all of these things perhaps patterns would have been recognised more quickly and perhaps we'd have been here sooner. But we didn't. However, we had a list of things that we were trying to raise with the senior management of the hospital, really to seek their advice as to how we could possibly go about investigating this. All we wanted was to know how to investigate these events properly.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Unfortunately, this is something that we are not taught at medical school or through our postgraduate training.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If someone does something to harm a baby, you just do nothing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We didn't do nothing, Mr Myers. We tried our best to escalate our concerns to the senior management of the hospital.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: First of all, you didn't escalate any concern with Ms Letby on this occasion, did you? You didn't say a word to her?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You didn't raise anything with the shift leader?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You didn't put a Datix complaint in?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: At any point, as it happens?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You don't make a note anywhere of what you're telling us happened, do you, in any record?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think the notes are very detailed. I mean --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You don't put a note in these records of what you're saying is a person of interest, standing there, acting suspiciously and potentially dislodging an ETT?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because that's not the one of thing one writes in medical notes -- and at the time I wasn't anticipating that several years later I'd be sitting here talking to you.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You have a duty to look after the children on your unit, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If you think someone is deliberately harming them, you act to protect them, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We did our best to act to protect them, as I say, by raising our concerns to the senior executive level medical management.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: At this point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Concerns were very first raised before this by my colleague Dr Brearey -- and in February, I can't remember whether it was before or after this, we raised them again.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I make it plain, I don't accept the accuracy or truth of any allegation against the defendant on her behalf, but I'm just going through this from what you're saying at the moment, Dr Jayaram, so we're not in any misunderstanding.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Lucy Letby continued to work on this department for another 4 months or so, didn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You were telling us last week about a discolouration that you claim you saw with [Baby M]; do you remember that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Another thing that you didn't make a note about at the time.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I explained that last time about not understanding the clinical significance.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You -- had you thought someone was actively involved in harming children on your unit, you would have not failed to raise it with the police.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If I may take a step back -- and I've already said this, Mr Myers. We had significant concerns, really probably certainly from the autumn of 2015. We escalated these concerns, they were on the radar of someone as senior as the executive director of nursing as far back as October 2015. As clinicians, we put our faith in the system, in our senior management, to guide us as to how to escalate these concerns and investigate them. The initial response was: it's very unlikely there's anything going on, see what happens. We said, okay, against our better judgement in retrospect.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We flagged it up again in the February to the medical director and the director of nursing that we had concerns and my colleague Dr Brearey, who was the neonatal lead, requested to have a meeting with them.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: They didn't respond to that for another 3 months. And we were stuck because we had concerns and we didn't know what to do.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In retrospect, we wish we had bypassed them and asked the police. All we wanted was to be advised as to the correct way forwards in terms of investigating this association. We by no means had played judge and jury at any point, but the association was becoming clearer and clearer and we needed to find the right way to do this.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: This is an unprecedented situation for us. Nobody trains us to deal with this. And as I have mentioned before, we work within a certain rulebook and a certain playing field. We are not thinking "Could this be deliberate harm" initially. And these thoughts come into your head after a while and you put them away because it seems utterly preposterous. Then more and more happens, and then it is very easy sometimes then to start seeing things that aren't there.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We are all aware of the concept of confirmation bias: if you buy a red car, you suddenly start noticing lots of red cars. But even taking into account that there was a risk of confirmation bias and we were seeing things that actually weren't there, these episodes were becoming more and more and more frequent with this association.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And yes, you know, in retrospect, it's easy, we should have put Datix forms in, we should have written these specific concerns maybe in the notes but we didn't. But eventually, it reached a point in June 2016 where we did say something has got to change, but that's not for me to talk about now.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Dealing with this specific incident you're describing to us, you raised no complaint with anyone at the time, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not to anybody on the neonatal unit, but I discussed this because I knew that we had a list of concerns already.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You made no formal record at the time, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't make a formal record at the time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And you and which other consultants are talking about are all grown adults who don't need to be trained to call the police if someone is hurting babies, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The trouble is at that time it was one of a list of possibilities and all we could see was the association.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And the significance --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And we also, as I've alluded to before, were under -were beginning to get a reasonable amount of pressure from the senior management of the hospital not to make a fuss. And in retrospect, yes, absolutely, we're grown-ups and we should have stood up and not listened.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And the significance of this event, if it happened in the way you said to the police some years later, is that this would have given you what you needed to make that complaint if you're telling the truth about it, Dr Jayaram, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Are you suggesting that I'm not telling the truth?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: First of all, do you agree, once this happened, if it happened the way you say, you were in a position to go and make something of this, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In this isolated incident, absolutely not, because it was an association, I didn't see her do anything.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I didn't see her do anything, but I still find it very difficult to understand why in that short period of time, when [Baby K] had been stable, poorly but stable, and Jo Williams left, she had this deterioration.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I also don't understand why an alarm didn't go off. And even if an alarm didn't go off, I don't understand, when it was clear she was desaturating, I wasn't called or someone hadn't raised an alarm.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You did nothing at the time, Dr Jayaram --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I resuscitated [Baby K].
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Nothing in terms of a complaint --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- because there was no suspicion that Ms Letby had interfered with anything or failed to act.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think there's an element --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That's the truth of it, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The truth of it is that we're thinking the unthinkable and, as with anyone, when one first hears about these things, you don't want to believe it, just as I had this instinct. And in retrospect, I wish we had. But actually, we did add it to the list of concerns that we wanted to discuss with senior hospital executive medical and nursing management for advice as to how to proceed.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And in retrospect, were I ever in such a situation again -- and I sincerely hope I never, ever am -- I would have no hesitation in bypassing the apparent correct lines of communication.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Because raising an issue, if things had happened the way you're telling us, is the obvious thing to do, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And you didn't, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We did. We raised it, as I say, with senior hospital management.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And in fact the suggestion that Ms Letby did the sort of things, or rather didn't do them in the way you're saying now,
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: is something that you said to the police years later when they interviewed you, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We'd been saying it or wondering about that association from that time and it took a long time for the police to be involved.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Could we look at tile 103, please, in the prosecution schedule of events? Can we just go behind that? This is in the sequence of events. This is the record of what takes place. It's a record from the network service the morning that we're dealing with.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I want to go down, it's in our sequence, can we go down, please, scroll down. 05.55. It says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Call received from Dr Jayaram. Baby dislodged the tune and had to be re-intubated." Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I would probably have said that the tube was dislodged, I don't think I'd have said the baby dislodged it. In the normal scheme of things, if a tube is going to be dislodged, it's most likely dislodged by the baby. But in a 25-weeker who's not vigorous and not moving around, with a tube that's in to a good length and secured, it's a very unlikely thing to happen and I don't know, if it did happen, it happened in that window.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: This is in the material that we have, Dr Jayaram. Do you agree if it says that -- do you agree you said that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't remember what words I used. That's what's been recorded there.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And actually, it's more likely in the general scheme of things that a baby would, but it's also very unlikely that a small 25-week gestation baby would have dislodged a tube. It can happen when babies are being handled; there was no reason for [Baby K] to have been handled. It can happen during cares. It can happen if a baby is very vigorous; that's usually with bigger, heavier, more robust, stronger babies. And in that situation, with somebody watching the baby, it would have been witnessed and it's likely to have been seen by the nurse looking after the baby.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: First of all, a baby like [Baby K], as she was at that point, is capable of dislodging a tube by her own movement, isn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Except she wasn't really moving very much and I think that's still very unlikely. It's possible, as is anything possible, but I don't think in my time looking after small premature babies that I have seen a baby at this stage who's not vigorous, with a tube that's secured, dislodge a tube.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you recall ever telling the police that tubes can get dislodged by very active babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It can happen but she wasn't a very active baby.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to come to that. Let's deal first of all in principle.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In principle, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: An active premature baby can dislodge a tube, can't she or he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If they're very active but a baby of this weight and this size at this stage...
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And actually, that's what you thought had happened at the time, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I thought the tube -- well, the tube had been dislodged because there's nothing else that could have been going on at that point.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And if you had seen Ms Letby doing or not doing what you say, you wouldn't be suggesting it was the baby that had dislodged the tube, would you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think when -- again, the thought in my head was, has this been done deliberately. I'm not going to say this to the receiving consultant at the other end. And I would probably have said that the tube was dislodged -- the interpretation would be that the baby had dislodged the tube because obviously the receiving consultant isn't going to assume that it has been done by anybody else.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We can take that down, thank you. You told the jury earlier on that the ventilator was not alarming.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct -- certainly that wasn't what prompted me. I would -- I didn't hear an alarm as I walked in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You've just given evidence this morning, the ventilator — you were asked about it, you were asked about the alarm, you said the ventilator was not alarming. That was your evidence, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It wasn't alarming and the monitor was not alarming either.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And a ventilator not alarming, you have -- that makes it sound more suspicious, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Potentially.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes. In fact, and you can look at this if it helps, isn't your actual recollection you can't recall whether it was sounding?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It wasn't sounding -- well, the reason I got up from where I was sitting wasn't because I heard an alarm going off. And in the anatomy of the neonatal unit, the alarms are loud and I would have gone in had I heard an alarm.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you dispute that the alarm sounded, Dr Jayaram?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't recall it going off and that's not why I went in. And certainly when I went in and I walked in, I don't remember the alarm going off because if the alarm had been going off, that's what would have prompted me to stand up and go through.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you remember having a conversation with Nurse Williams when you went over at some point after the desaturation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I... I will have had a conversation to sort of say, you know, her tube's out and we've had to -- and she desaturated and we've had to re-intubate her, but I can't remember when Nurse Williams came back, at what point in the proceedings she came back.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You asked her, "Who was in the room when the alarm went off?" That's something you said to her, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't remember.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You asked her what had happened; do you recall that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I asked Ms Williams?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you recall asking --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She wasn't in the room when I went in -- was this for the first incident?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: No. After the first incident, do you recall asking Joanne Williams what had happened?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, because she wasn't in the room.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She might have asked me what happened.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Because if things happened in the way you're saying, you wouldn't need to ask Joanne Williams, who came back later, what had happened, would you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't ask. I didn't -- well, why would I have asked her what happened? Because she wasn't in the room when it happened.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to suggest you did ask her who was there when the alarm went off because you heard an alarm go, you could hear an alarm ringing.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. I don't recall that at all. That's not my recollection in the slightest because had I heard an alarm going, that would have been the prompt for me to go in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You're able to give quite a precise timing for how long Joanne Williams had been gone for by the time you went to the room, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Roughly, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You said 2 to 2.5 minutes --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think so.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- this morning, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we look at tile 63, it shows us the swipe data. If we go behind that, we can see the swipe data for Joanne Williams is that she left the neonatal unit to go to the labour ward at 3.47. So she had left 3 minutes before the desaturation. So your timing of about 2 to 2.5 minutes after she went is pretty spot on, isn't it? I mean, do you always have a memory that's that precise, Dr Jayaram?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In this event I did because I just remember that, as I described, what I felt was this irrational discomfort and I kept telling myself, don't be ridiculous, and looking at my watch. But you know, it was a feeling -- and actually I'm saying 2 to 2.5 minutes, I didn't have a stopwatch on it. So it's, you know, guesswork that it was around that, but I think it was.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It seems to dovetail with the swipe data very neatly, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have never seen the swipe data in my life. I don't have any reason to look at swipe data and I don't have -- I wouldn't have access to swipe data were I even wanting to look at it. I'm trying to work out why you think this is important. I know you don't like me asking you questions.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It's not that I don't like it, but his Lordship will tell you, the general way of business here is that we have t ask the questions and the jury are helped by you answering them, so would you do that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But it would help me to answer your questions if I understood the kind of things that you are getting at because it would help me frame how I answer your questions.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes. You'd like to know where we're going before I ask the question?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not really. It just really helps me to understand how you're thinking -- in my professional practice we have two-way adult discussions and we actually treat each other as equals. Now, I appreciate in this situation this is different and it is quite difficult for me. And I appreciate I'm probably speaking out of turn, but it would help me to answer your questions.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Let me get back to the questions. I have asked you about this timing. You made statements to the police dealing with this incident -- I've got them in front of me -- on 17 April 2018, Dr Jayaram --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- 12 June 2018, 4 June 2021, and 15 February 2022.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right? In none of them do you suggest it's 2.5 or -- sorry, 2 to 2.5 minutes that Joanne Williams had been away for. Do you accept that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... Do I give a time at all in those statements?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I accept that it's not mentioned in those statements then.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We can check. If I'm wrong, I'll be corrected, you can be sure of that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When you were interviewed by the police before this in April 2018, before those statements, and perhaps you -- you said this and you can be shown it if you want to see it. It's at page K9662.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we scroll down on this particular topic. Can you see that? You say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I can't remember how long Jo Williams had been out of the room before this happened. It was the middle of the night, over 2 years ago." Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now, just a couple of years after this event you were able to tell the police how long Jo Williams had been out of the room for; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was an estimate, and it's probably about right --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You said --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- because at the time I subsequently thought about it.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: But I think regardless, you're focusing again on minutiae. The point is that this event happened in that window that she was out.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: One of the things that I'm going to suggest you have done, Dr Jayaram, is to take certain details and add them to what you say as you've gone along; is that clear?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's clear and I would disagree with that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: On this occasion I'm suggesting one thing you have done is, wherever you've got it from, you have picked up the time Joanne Williams is away and worked that into your account later on. Do you agree or disagree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I absolutely disagree with that because I would not have seen any data, unless I'd been asked a leading question by the police, which would be documented in this transcript. Absolutely not. I find it preposterous, really, that you're suggesting such a thing.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Can you help us how it was that in April of 2018, when talking about this, you have told the police you couldn't remember how long she'd been out of the room, it's in the middle of the night 2 years ago, and now, about 7 years later, you're
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: telling us it's about 2.5 minutes that she was out of the room? How's that happened?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because I've had more time to reflect on it.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And your memory's improved in the period in between, has it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The events of this night are emblazoned and I don't know why I specifically didn't say that. This was in the context of a very long conversation about a lot of things.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You change things as you go along, Dr Jayaram, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: [Baby K] was a poorly baby because of her prematurity, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And her management and care at the Countess of Chester on your watch, I'm going to suggest, agree or disagree as you wish, fell below the standard that she required?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I disagree. There were things, absolutely, that we could have done better in terms of intubation, et cetera, but I disagree entirely that the care she received was detrimental. She was a poorly baby. She was a premature baby with a history of prolonged ruptured membranes, possible risk factors for infection, and she behaved in a way that one would expect a 25week gestation baby to behave. The only thing to me that doesn't compute is that first deterioration.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The other events are events that can be seen with babies that are premature and I think they were managed as well as we could have done in the circumstances. As I said, this is why ideally babies that are born very prematurely should be born in a tertiary centre.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Unfortunately, sometimes, that can't happen, and I don't -- I refute the allegation that the care that we provided influenced the ultimate outcome. Others may disagree.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Have you sought to distract from what I'm suggesting to you are shortcomings in her care at least in part by creating this issue about Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm sorry, can I just frame what you're suggesting? So what you're suggesting is that I, and possibly my colleagues -are you talking just with reference to this case or other cases?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm asking about this incident at this point, Dr Jayaram.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What you're suggesting is that I am trying to distract everybody from what you perceive as the extremely poor care provided by myself and my team by focusing on this one incident. Is that what you're suggesting?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You've added the word "extremely". But what I'm asking you is have you sought to distract from what I'm suggesting is a poor level of care by creating this issue?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's an easy question to answer: absolutely not.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And are you seeking to bolster suspicion against Lucy Letby by adding details after the event?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely not.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You agree, [Baby K] should have been at a tertiary centre, shouldn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In an ideal world, in different circumstances, if this had been anticipated, she'd have been born in a tertiary centre, but we know that can't happen every time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Well, there was some warning when [Baby K] was going to be born, wasn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a decision made by the obstetricians and the midwives who decide whether a mother is transferred with the baby in utero.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We've seen that there was a spontaneous rupture of membranes 48 hours before the delivery, wasn't there; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now, when you contacted the tertiary centre in the early hours that morning, you were told there was a bed ready, a bed available, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was told that for the baby, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And Arrowe Park is a 20-minute drive from the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's not my decision or a paediatrician's decision around whether a mother is transferred before the baby is born. We will always try our best to get the obstetricians to transfer, but it's not my decision or a paediatric decision as
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: to whether a mother is safe enough to transport or not. We have no say in that matter.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you agree that the hospital should have ensured that [Baby K] could be born in a tertiary if there was a bed available?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know the circumstances of the discussions with the obstetricians. I'm not an obstetrician, I'm not a midwife, I don't understand what the issues were with [Baby K]'s mother's clinical decision that led them to make the decision that, on balance, she was too unstable to transfer. I can't answer that. It's not within my field of expertise.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And let me then ask: as a consultant of many years' experience, who has worked at that hospital for a long time, do you agree that on the face of it there appeared to time and opportunity to make that arrangement?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Given that there was 48 hours, but I don't know at what stage [Baby K]'s mother presented to the obstetricians and again I can't comment on the clinical decision-making of that specialty, it's not my expertise.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The chances of survival for a baby like [Baby K] are improved if she is at a tertiary centre, aren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They are improved, absolutely, which is why ideally they are born at tertiary centres. But unfortunately sometimes that isn't possible.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And there is no time to waste in terms of getting them there if that can be effected, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: [Baby K] didn't arrive until about quarter past 3 on the 17th that afternoon?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: To the tertiary centre?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Some of that -- again, you will have to talk to the transport team and the team at Arrowe Park -- is about how stable babies are to transport as well. By this stage she was having issues with her blood pressure, she was needing inotropic medication to maintain her blood pressure, and it is far safer to optimise ventilation, to optimise blood pressure before transport, as best as is possible. Sometimes it's not possible and the transport teams just have to pick up and run. But it's
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: standard practice for transport teams -- although I'm saying this, I don't work on a transport team and I haven't for a very, very long time -- to get a baby as stable as possible before transfer, so the fact that she didn't leave the unit until later that day is neither here nor there. The team that were down, the transport team, are the tertiary team so she was receiving care from people with that expertise.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The standard of care that she received in the first few hours of her life is capable of having an impact upon her chances of survival going forwards, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Intubation, let me ask you about that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If I suggest to you intubation should be achieved within about a 15-minute period of birth where it's an emergency intubation, do you agree or disagree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would agree ideally, but the important thing in this situation was that in the periods where she wasn't intubated, she was adequately ventilated, as evidenced by the fact that her chest was moving and her saturations picked up.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The guidance that it should be achieved within 15 minutes takes into account the fact that a baby will be intubated -- it will be given oxygen as that process goes along, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but they can receive that through a T-piece and mask as well. The only advantage of earlier intubation is you'll get your surfactant slightly earlier and actually the recommendation is if you can't intubate or intubation is difficult, then don't just keep trying if you've got a secure airway.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: One of the reasons intubation took the time that it did was that it was undertaken by a relatively junior registrar, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: By James Smith.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes. He was a relatively junior registrar, an ST5, wasn't he.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As an ST5 he will have done at least a year of tertiary neonatal practice where he will have developed intubation skills. And if any of our junior trainees, our registrars -- and I don't like the term junior because it implies they're quite
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: green but they are experienced. We make an assessment together with them of their competence. If Dr Smith had said, "I don't feel comfortable doing this, please will you do it", I would have done it, but we also have to take these opportunities to train. This isn't experimenting on babies, this is standard practice. And it's important for him to have these skills -- and actually even experienced intubators sometimes will struggle occasionally to get a tube down.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You told us this morning this was a tricky technique and more difficult in smaller babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You also told us, as you proceeded, it was trickier than anticipated.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You should have taken over, shouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would have taken over at the point where Dr Smith was struggling. I could see that actually he could do this and he did it safely. He never went more than 30 seconds, because we follow standard practice, and he maintained [Baby K]'s airway absolutely impeccably and ventilated her there through the Tpiece impeccably as well.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you agree it would have been preferable for you to take over when he was struggling to achieve this when it was trickier than anticipated?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's something that I could have done but I also -it's important not to undermine his confidence as well. And all of these things are a judgement call at the time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If [Baby K] at that point -- and we'd been in a situation where we were actually struggling to ventilate her with the T-piece, so for example when we'd put the mask over her face and ventilate her through the T-piece and we weren't getting gas in and out of her lungs and we weren't maintaining her heart rate and we weren't keeping her saturations up then absolutely at that point I would have taken over.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Because this is trickier than anticipated, you used a 2 millimetre rather than a 2.5, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And we know, we've seen it, there was quite a high air leak after intubation, wasn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Is that insignificant?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As I've explained, the point -- the leak is a measured value, it's looking at how much gas goes through the tube, through the hole in the tube and how much comes out, and it calculates the difference between the two.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So 94% leak is significant in the context that if we're struggling to ventilate a baby then actually she would benefit from a bigger tube. But we had a secure airway with relatively minimal pressures on the ventilator, we were moving the chest, and had reasonable blood gases and reasonable saturations. So actually the leak in itself is there but it's not of clinical significance in terms of the baby.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If, with that leak, we'd seen that [Baby K] was needing increasing amounts of oxygen, we were having to put increased -higher and higher pressures through the ventilator to ventilate her then, yes, absolutely. But actually the number itself has to be put in the context of the bigger picture.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Surfactant should be delivered within certainly, at the latest, 5 minutes of intubation, shouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Ideally, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now, we can look at the timings, but we have seen a prescription for surfactant at 3 o'clock, but I will go to an earlier timing that we have, the earliest timing that we've got, which is at tile 31, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just as we find that, the reason it has to be done quickly is surfactant is to assist the lungs in the elasticity they need for respiration to take place, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What surfactant does is it lines the alveoli, the air sacs, and if you don't have surfactant, they have a tendency at the end of every breath to collapse down completely, so rather like my analogy of the balloon earlier on, so each time a baby breathes, it's like the beginning of a balloon. So surfactant is normally produced by cells in the lung in the alveolar lining.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The surfactant we give from the outside is to support the baby — and we try to give it as early as possible.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And it's to ensure that respiration happens effectively, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It improves gas exchange --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And that --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- and ventilation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That's the reason why, in a small baby like this, it's got to be quick that it's delivered --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The sooner the better, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Because minutes without having the lungs working as effectively as they can can be damaging in the long run, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, what's damaging in the long run is having prolonged periods with low oxygen saturations and not being able to ventilate. So if surfactant is given slightly later than anticipated in the situation where a baby is oxygenating adequately I would contend it doesn't make that much difference in the long run. What makes a difference in the long run is a prolonged period of having low oxygen saturations.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We're going to go behind this tile just to look at the timing we have here. If we just scroll down, further down the page, keep scrolling down, thank you. On to the next page. Is this your handwriting on this page, Dr Jayaram?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: All right. We can see surfactant given. It's got a dose of 120 milligrams. And the date, 17 February, time 02.45. Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If the intubation took 20 minutes it would have been complete at 2.32. If the intubation took 12 minutes, which is what it says in the nursing notes, it would have been completed by 2.24. It may seem to be a matter of minutes but as it happens, it comes late, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's later than it could have been, yes, but I would contend it made no difference because subsequently, if we look at [Baby K]'s ventilator settings and what she was on, she was on a relatively low pressures -- and 50% oxygen sounds like a lot of oxygen, but for a 25-week gestation baby that's not a
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: huge amount and actually her oxygen requirement came down slightly after she had surfactant. So I think really focusing on whether she had surfactant earlier or later, absolutely it could have been given earlier, but with reference to the episode that happened when the tube was dislodged, it is not relevant to it whatsoever.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So we can keep track of what is or isn't relevant -- the jury will decide that, Dr Jayaram -- we are looking at two matters here. One of them is any potential cumulative effect of any shortcomings, so we can keep track. And the second matter is what the quality of care was in the unit and gauging it by the way that help is given. Do you understand that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So putting to one side, for the time being, what the consequences may be, the surfactant has come late, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's later than we would have liked, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The intubation has taken longer than would have been ideal?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It has, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And where we began, ideally, [Baby K] should have been born in a tertiary unit if that could have been done?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Ideally.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Let's carry on. You're familiar with the concept of the golden hour, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: They are the steps that should be taken early in a neonate's life, within the first hour of life, aren't they --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- to improve the outcomes. That's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And again it's because the accumulation of small shortcomings may lead to a large shortcoming in the long run, mightn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's -- potentially, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Also, a unit that is acting effectively and delivering the right level of care should be aiming to meet the requirements of the golden hour, shouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I would like to look at the notes, just some of the entries on the notes that you made, Dr Jayaram. So if we go, please, to -- I'll check which tile. Tile 65, please, Mr Murphy. You, we know, wrote these notes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Dr Smith had been giving the treatment, hadn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Is there any particular reason why you wrote the notes when it was Dr Smith who had given the treatment?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know, I can't remember. Quite often in this situation we would both write records. I don't know whether Dr Smith wrote anything or not.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In fact, could we go to the top of this tile. We went through these, I'm not going to go through all the entries here, but just a couple of them. These are set out -- the note was written at 04.50 retrospectively.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We've seen the first page deals with happened on delivery and on the way to the -- prior to the neonatal unit. This page says "on arrival"; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, so once we had got [Baby K] established on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: All right. And on arrival it's got a series of steps that are taken set out, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It has.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And reading through it, it would appear these are steps that are taken sequentially on arrival in the unit; is that what it conveys?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It conveys that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It does? And if we just scroll down to the bottom of this page, we can see this page ends with the desaturation at 03.50, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So what you are conveying with this page is what was done prior to 03.50 in [Baby K]'s care on this unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what it conveys, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: However, I will say, having seen the morphine prescription chart, I would say that it does look like the morphine infusion was not commenced until later.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We'll come to morphine in a little bit, Dr Jayaram. Can we just look at the antibiotics. First, if we scroll up -sorry, about the up and down, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we just look up, antibiotics. Under the principles of good and effective care, Dr Jayaram, antibiotics should be delivered within that first hour, shouldn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And certainly, looking at the way this note is set out, we can see where the reference to antibiotics is
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (overspeaking) the line says sepsis.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Commenced IV penicillin and gentamicin." Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So that plainly conveys the message that, as expected, antibiotics have been delivered at the right time, doesn't it? Now we can see when this takes place if we look at tiles 79 and 80, please. We have the electronic prescriptions behind these. Gentamicin at 04.40 and we can see next to it penicillin at 04.40.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Do you have the prescription chart to say when they were written up? I accept if they were given then they were given later than they should have been, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we can to help you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)

If we could go, please, to -- I'm afraid I'll have to give you the J number, Mr Murphy, 17069. We have the tile number, it's 82. It seems to be the first one that we come to for gentamicin, Dr Jayaram. It's a little bit difficult, but we need to enlarge the top half of this form if we could, please. We can see:
"Patient details: [Baby K], baby girl. Date of birth, 17 February." Can you see it says gentamicin?

Yes. So that wasn't my signature, so it wasn't me that wrote it up. I'm guessing that was James Smith, I'm not sure, but I can't see on there what time it was prescribed. I can see what time it was given and I'll accept they were given later than they should have been.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: "Time given: 04.45" that says, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If that's right, that's come late, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's late. That's later than they should have been.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Although your note would appear to indicate it arrived in the right time frame, didn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And I think when I wrote my note it was on the assumption, wrongly, that they would have been certainly written up and delivered. I don't know why they were given later. Obviously there were -- there was the event that happened but that happened sort of after that first hour, so I accept that those antibiotics could have been given earlier.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And should have been given earlier; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Vitamin K is something that should be dealt with within the first hour, shouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Ideally. It's not as crucial. We give it as soon as possible.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I am just looking at the notes that you provide and the care that we have and the vitamin K appears to have been given, from your note, in advance of the desaturation, doesn't it, in that one-hour period?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think so. Again, it would have been written up -- I don't know time it was physically given. But the antibiotics
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: being given late is important. I don't think the vitamin K being given late would have had any bearing on events.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The vitamin K, we have it -- on the tile we have the record it was given at 04.20 in the morning. That's tile 72, which is outside the time frame for giving it, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I do want to turn to the morphine. I won't spend long with those. My Lord, I don't know whether you'd wish me to deal with that now or take our break now and carry on. I'm in the court's hands.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Are you likely to be more than about 5 minutes?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, I think I am likely to be more than 5 minutes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We'll have the break now then.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (A short break)
(In the absence of the jury)
My Lord, I know the witness is still in the box, but could we raise a housekeeping matter, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord was told earlier that we need to deal with Dr Babarao today. It may well be that we need to sit a little later than 4.30 if that's the case.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, we will sit late until it's finished.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Dr Jayaram, I'd be grateful if you could look with us at tile 65, which is from the clinical notes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It deals with what was done and when in that first section.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If we just scroll down a little bit to where it says meds, please, can you see, Dr Jayaram, it says morphine at 20 milligrams (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I can.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- micrograms, is it, per kilogram per hour?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Micrograms per kilogram per hour.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Micrograms per kilogram per hour. That certainly conveys the impression that morphine had been given prior to the desaturation, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It does. And having seen the prescription chart, I would say that that actually didn't happen at that time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: No. Now, I asked you a little earlier about the possibility of babies being able to dislodge the tubes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You agree that is possible?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is possible.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What you were anxious to explain to the police when you made the statement I've referred to in 17 April 2018 was in [Baby K]'s case, she had been sedated.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's absolutely correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Therefore she couldn't have dislodged it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I will absolutely agree that the timing of things, having seen that prescription chart, was different, and again from the way things are recorded there, that's correct, she wasn't on a morphine infusion. However, she was not a baby that had been very vigorous and trying to pull tubes out. Babies don't, at this gestation, consciously go for their tubes. And even though she wasn't on a morphine infusion at that time, I still contend that the probability of that tube doing what it did at the time that it did was unlikely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You were at pains to convey to the police that it was unlikely because she was sedated; that's what you were saying, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what I thought at the time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And let's be absolutely clear: you told them morphine stops the baby from being active and reduces the risk of tubes being dislodged?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It reduces the risk. The risk is small anyway.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You were explaining morphine would reduce it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And makes it less likely she could have knocked it herself?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And I accept now, looking at the timings of things, the morphine infusion was not running at that time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And you also said [Baby K] was a baby on sedation and was not moving around?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And I admit that at that time she wasn't but she wasn't vigorous. So generally, had -- in retrospect, and you can accuse me of changing things, but having seen that, I will absolutely accept that the morphine infusion, from what has been written, was not running at the time of the dislodgement. Had she been very vigorous, we almost certainly would have started that sooner. Again, I'm surprised it hadn't been started, but it hadn't been.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You added that detail -- first of all, you agree she wasn't actually sedated at all, was she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: From what I can see from those notes, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: She wasn't. You agree you told the police and emphasised that she was sedated?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You did that to support the impression you wanted to create that somebody else had interfered with that tube, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that's not why I did it. In good faith I thought at the time that the baby was on a morphine infusion at that time. And -- but even if she wasn't, there was nothing to suggest in the way she was behaving, up until the point that Jo Williams went to the labour ward, that she was vigorous or fighting or at risk of dislodging the tube. And if she had been, this certainly would have been started earlier.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It also follows, as it happens, morphine was not given at the point your notes appear to convey, was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
