blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to suggest what you have done is try to shift your evidence to try to take account of the fact that you didn't give morphine in the way you first said.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Have you tried to shift your evidence to take account of that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you describe what you mean by shift evidence?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Change it, try and account for the fact that you can't blame this on morphine now.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm still --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'll be clearer. I suggest you sought to convey to the police that [Baby K] couldn't move because she was sedated.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think at the time I gave that statement that was one of the things, but even accounting for the fact that she wasn't on a morphine infusion at that time, she was a 25-week gestation who had been born and needed resuscitation and she was not behaving in a way where we were worried she might pull a tube out, as had been reported. And until that moment that Jo Williams left she'd been absolutely stable, poorly but stable.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In your evidence, at a relatively early stage, the prosecution showed you that prescription for the infusion with your handwriting --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- and your signature at 03.50, didn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes. You appreciate that trying to say that [Baby K] can't move because she was on morphine simply can't be sustained now?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's not correct, I agree.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What you have said now is, well, it wasn't -- [Baby K] was not a vigorous baby is what you have said now; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: As it happens, that's not an observation you included, certainly in your statement, is it, that she wasn't a vigorous baby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What you said to them was because she was on morphine she couldn't move?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's one of the things, yes, I acknowledge that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And as it happens, before she was sedated, [Baby K] was actually quite an active little baby, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Define active. She could move but she wasn't making any purposeful movements and certainly she was not making any movements to actually dislodge a tube. To dislodge a tube you need to be able to either grab on to it and hook it out or be able to roll around enough. blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You deliberately misstated what happened with the morphine, Dr Jayaram, to make it sound as if it was less likely that [Baby K] (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I didn't deliberately misstate -- it was a genuine misunderstanding because I went from my notes, which obviously were written retrospectively. I wasn't aware, because I hadn't seen that prescription chart, that the morphine was not given until 3.50. And I accept that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I don't accept that I deliberately made an error or deliberately did that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: As it happens, not being sedated, [Baby K] was perfectly capable of moving in some way that could dislodge a tube?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's a possibility, but in a 25-week gestation baby who's 600 grams, the likelihood is very, very small.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And the fact that it happened in that small window of time is also of concern.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Your suggestion she was inactive is a detail that you have put in once you realised you can no longer stick with saying that she was sedated by means of morphine? That's what you have done?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She was not a baby that was jumping around, that we were concerned that she would dislodge a tube.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Just pausing, if we move on, on the question of blockage, are you aware the nursing notes make reference to there being secretions of blood and oral secretions?

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Babarao, I see it's late but we're going to try and deal with your evidence today. My Lord, I'll probably be 20 or 25 minutes to deal with this.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Again, we've just been dealing with the very sad situation here. I make it plain, as I have done before, the questions I ask are not meant to be insensitive in any way.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I appreciate that.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: We all appreciate what we're dealing with, but I need to deal with a number of topics.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The first thing is this, please, Dr Babarao. You are a consultant neonatologist, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: We've heard from consultant paediatricians in this case.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is a consultant neonatologist the same thing as a consultant paediatrician or is it a different type of specialty, could you explain to us?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Neonatology is a sub-specialty in paediatrics. So we train specifically to become a neonatologist. That's part of a three-year training programme in neonatology and other relevant
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: sub-specialties to get that sub-specialty recognition as a neonatologist.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Why is it -- what's the benefit of having that training, what difference does it make? This is so we can all understand.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In simplistic terms, when I become a neonatologist I care for the most extreme and complex newborn babies, including surgical and cardiac preterm and term babies.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: And I no longer care for children, so I specialise only in treating babies.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Is there a particular period of life that a neonatologist covers? A paediatrician might be everything up to the age of 16 years, but is there a particular period that a neonatologist focuses on and is dedicated to in their training and experience?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As a neonatologist, we cater to babies born from about 22 weeks' gestation until the point the baby gets home from the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Right. When you say "gets home from the neonatal unit", that means whatever gestation they were born at?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: After they leave the neonatal unit, you care for them up until that point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, in terms of care perspective. But we do follow them up until a period of 2 years to look at how they get on with weight, neurodevelopment, et cetera.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: So you will have specialist experience in training in babies in the earliest years of life?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: And paediatricians who are employed more generally across maternity units or paediatric units may not have that focused level of expertise?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Do you agree that the outcome for [Baby K] may have been better if she'd been born at a tertiary centre?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's the evidence.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: It makes a difference, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Your understanding of the notes that you've seen is that there should have been what's called an in utero transfer, shouldn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's the intention.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Yes, the intention.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Because it was important that [Baby K] should be at a tertiary centre, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: And in utero, of course, means before she had been born?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: In fact, did you find any clear explanation why that didn't happen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can only refer to the notes, what I had documented there. There was an opportunity for an in utero transfer. I extrapolated what I believe is -- because [Baby K] was able to come to the neonatal unit, so the reason for declining an in utero transfer could have been maternity beds at the time at Arrowe Park Hospital and that could be related to staffing or there was no physical space, I don't know.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Right. Is that to say it's not quite clear why she wasn't transferred?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: But the bottom line is she should have been if there was any way of doing that; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. The other reason could have been that [Baby K]'s mother may not have been stable enough for a transfer.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Again, I can't comment on that because I have not documented that information.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Once she'd been born at the Countess of Chester, clinically was it important for her to be transferred to the tertiary unit as quickly as possible?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Realistically, yes.
blocks.speaker: BABARAO

blocks.text: Realistically. We know that she arrived at 13.15. With a baby like [Baby K], the sooner she gets there, the better. The sooner she gets to the tertiary unit, the better, isn't it?

blocks.text: Yes, but safely.

blocks.text: And safely. The difference in the hours of care she spends at a tertiary can improve her chances if she gets there hours earlier; do you agree?

blocks.text: All right. I just want to ask you about one of the entries in the notes that we looked at. It was at tile 140, please. Could we go behind this? Pausing there, I want to be clear about something you just said, that as a matter of principle, Dr Babarao, the outcomes for a baby are invariably better if born at a tertiary unit; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: I don't want there to be any misunderstanding from your last answer.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's only the parameters of the golden hour. So what's being done to a preterm baby just after birth -- things have changed in the last few years.
